questions.q: What does a single artificial neuron compute, before its activation function is applied?
options: A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias
The average of all training labels
A random number used to break ties
The number of layers in the network
questions.explain: A neuron's pre-activation value z is w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ... + b — the same weighted-sum-plus-bias arithmetic as linear regression.

questions.q: In the lesson's worked example, inputs x1=0.5 and x2=0.8 go into a neuron with w1=0.3, w2=0.9, b=0.1. What is z?
In the two-neuron hidden layer example, what do h1 and h2 represent?
options: A new, learned representation built from the inputs
questions.explain: h1 and h2 are each hidden neuron's activated output — a new representation the network builds, not the raw x1/x2 values.

questions.q: Why does adding a hidden layer with a nonlinear activation matter?
options: It makes training faster in every case
It removes the need for a loss function
It guarantees the model will not overfit
It lets the model bend a straight decision line into a curve, instead of only drawing straight lines
questions.explain: Without nonlinearity, stacking layers collapses back into one linear function. The activation is what lets hidden layers build genuinely new, curved decision boundaries.

questions.q: In a multi-layer forward pass, what does the output layer's neuron use as its input?
options: The outputs of the previous layer's neurons
questions.explain: Each layer's output becomes the next layer's input — the output neuron in the example reads h1 and h2, not x1 and x2, directly.
